meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Owen found out about a zero on his phone, in class. Who decided that?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
Pretty conclusive. A machine's guess, Hale, and Turnitin's own guide says it shouldn't be the sole basis for punishing a student; I have it printed in my bag. What else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Now show me what you actually have on the essay.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.

11:31, 11:52, 11:58; I'm writing those down. Owen told me he wrote it over the weekend, and a finished draft pasted into a fresh document at night proves nothing about who wrote it. Under 4.3, you also consider his process and his other work, so what else?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Turn it toward me. A seventeen-year-old misremembering a line is a careless quotation, not proof of anything. Whatever comes next, Hale, this stays off his record and it stays quiet.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Kids change their thesis between an outline and the final draft; that's what an outline is for. So what exactly are you proposing, Hale?

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Five minutes after class, a seventeen-year-old put on the spot, written up by you; that's your impression, not a document. Send me the version history and the outline tonight. And I asked what you're proposing.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

Then Owen does the rewrite, privately, to put this behind him and for no other reason. I want it scheduled and marked well before December 1, and nothing on file, in your email tonight. Which day, Hale?
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school, and all of it in your email tonight.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, provided your email tonight says it's private, it replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed today that Owen will complete a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, that its mark will replace the zero and be entered well before December 1, and that nothing will be placed on his record. I still require all of this confirmed in writing, including that the rewrite is private and not in front of his class. I expect your email tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: last position; she agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12 after school, with its mark replacing the zero before December 1, and she still wants your written confirmation tonight that it stays private and nothing goes on his record, which is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, reached well before her time ran out.
What moved her: you showed the version history with its exact times and no earlier drafts, because it was dated, tied to his own work and something she could check on your screen.
What cost ground: you opened by calling the checker score conclusive, because a software number is the one thing she came prepared to dismiss and it made her start harder.
What she never said: one night in October she came downstairs at 1 AM, saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the whole essay between 11:31 PM and 11:58 PM on October 28, the night before it was due, which came very close to that night, though it proves nothing about the essay and is only why she fought so hard.
Try next time: open with owning the November 3 zero and turning the screen to the version history, and leave the checker score out entirely.
